lede: An ironic and lucid association between the journeys of Saint John and Beuys: both prophets in the desert, announcing a message whose complete meaning makes sense only in the future, in the light of subsequent events.
about.0:
An ironic and lucid association between the journeys of St. John and Beuys: both
were prophets in the desert, announcing a message whose complete significance would make
sense only in the future, in the light of subsequent events. Beuys really is an appropriate
choice to illustrate the difficulty of transmitting art in modernity. As Angel González says,
“a piece by Duchamp produces interpretations, one by Matisse,
sensations. Nevertheless, an image by Beuys
generates new images, as if Beuys’s images lacked
something: they were incomplete. It is not, then, or so it seems
to me, a case of pedagogic hypnosis, but rather of the persuasive exhibition of
something imperfect, insufficient, unresolved.”
Mercedez Replinger extract from the book Instalações Barja - 2005, from the text “Uncertain documents in place of the monster”.
trecho.0: That is how he appropriates icons and myths, texts and objects, concepts and bodies of knowledge; artists and prophets, poets and thinkers are also summoned. They are like characters to be recombined in this vast and mundane library. He selects them and associates them in improbable, at times laughable ways that unveil the arbitrariness of signs and discourses, the blind spots that have always startled the arts, the illegibilities that have haunted them. References that at first would seem to us disparate are gradually sutured, producing new meanings, other abysses. John the Baptist meets another John, Beuys; Goethe’s sun/eye becomes the fifth musical note of the C major scale, sol, opening itself to the ear; the eye, privileged organ of knowledge and of vertical transcendence (from Plato’s sun to the divine light) is converted into Bataille’s eye-anus. In the interval between the visible and the invisible, the said and the silenced, revelation and blindness, language and the world, the usual nexuses are broken. An interval that welcomes the opacities in order to open art to unlimited encounters, but that does not cease to confide its indeterminacy and its misfits. trecho.3: CULTURE X NATURE = BARBA- RISM - The animal is foreign par excellence, the truly incomprehensible other. The equation seems concluded: “Cultura X Natureza = Barbárie” (1997-2004). In the end, two incompatible elements provoke destruction. In a certain way the artist seems to place before our eyes the negative of the romantic dream that Beuys represented, his confidence in the possibility of using the energy of animals to reach the desired unity that, much earlier, had already been announced, for example, by Schiller when he envied the Greeks’ proximity to nature: “they are what we were; they are what we must become again. We have been nature like them, and our culture must return by the path of reason and freedom to nature”. Mercedes Replinger González extract from the book Instalações Barja - 2005; from the text “Uncertain documents in place of the monster”.

trecho.5: Barja’s works, a series of Brazilian and European theoreticians and artists: Evgene Bavcar, Mercedes Replinger, Adolfo Montejo Navas, Roland Campos, Angélica Madeira, Bené Fonteles and Marília Panitz produced an important body of reflections that accompany this compilation of records that survived time. It is possible, in this way, to travel here through twenty years of history by means of the projects and installations: “Experiência Tumulto (1985)”, “Cubo Cruz Lápide (1985)”, “O Profeta e a Jaguatirica (1985-86)”, “DO AKD-MICO AO POLE-MICO (1986)”, “Mognus Dei (1990)”, “O Sol de Goethe (1999)”, “São João Beuys (1990)”, “Ser ou não Ser, Ao Gullar (1993)”, “Pega Manet/De Onde Vem A Escuridão (1986)”, “TV Anal (1999)”, “Hermógenes (1999)”, “Obranome (2003)” and “Cultura X Natureza = Barbárie (1998/2005)” Marília Panitz, in her text “To What Matters, an Answer”, proposes an itinerary for reading Barja’s works, starting from the concept of equation, so dear to the artist. In the “enigmas of visual equations” of Barja’s commentaries-constructions, the author highlights the condensation of meanings that has humour as its tool. Angélica Madeira, in commenting on the installation “São João Beuys”, draws attention to the infinity of associations and meanings existing between the immortal and charismatic political agitators that Saint John the Baptist and Joseph Beuys were. Angélica Madeira highlights the influence of surrealism and dada in this work, in which coexist the playful, of a supposedly unpretentious humour, and the gravity of the materials, above all the mutton fat which, under the action of light, solidifies and liquefies over the course of the day, causing strangeness and unease. trecho.9: a history; also, a language that incontestably speaks to us. We will approach Wagner Barja’s work precisely through this gaze, which is a listening, by means of an itinerary traced by some concrete works and installations that, among other themes, are interrelated by certain aspects: the problem of the visibility and invisibility of the work, from the metaphors of light to those of blindness; the passage from image and text to the object. Lastly, the explicit homages to his cultural and artistic past, of which he feels an heir, in conflict. From Ferreira Gullar, Lygia Clark, J. Beuys to Aleijadinho; that is, it follows a trajectory from the avant-gardes to the roots proper to the Brazilian baroque. This division does not imply a strict separation, since all these themes and concepts appear, to a greater or lesser degree, in each of the pieces and installations, which represent in themselves an excess and a residue that unfolds in the following work and generates a continuous process of metamorphoses, thus underlining the open character of artistic creation. To look, in this sense, necessarily implies theorizing, generating a thought that is built with the very movement of the eyes. As Goethe had already pointed out:

However, the trait of the fictitious animal is evidenced in the human projection of an anguish and a terror before these impenetrable beings, completely foreign to man, which the animals are, all of them, including those familiar and domestic. In this way, this marvellous fauna, alliance of a dream and a nightmare, is the symptom of the limits of man’s reality. Between one frontier and the other, God’s and Man’s, we may think that the thing in itself, the object by itself, is capable of distilling a living organism: a hybrid body, like the strange animal that Barja proposes in “São João Beuys” (1990), unusual metamorphosis of a small oratory, of those used in homes for popular devotion, in this case dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, transmuted into an animal with a large tail of lambskin. If “OBRANOME” annulled the distances between image and word, name and thing, “São João Beuys” (1990) fuses inert matter with the living specimen, whose silent faces shelter in their interior a small golden vessel with mutton tallow, situated strategically: during the day, the sunlight melts the tallow, which returns to the solid state during the night.
